Ursula von der Leyen, President of the European Commission, will present the annual State of the Union address to the European Parliament in Strasbourg on Wednesday. The speech, scheduled for 9 a.m. Paris time (GMT+2), will be broadcast live on France 24, offering EU legislators and the public a direct view of the Commission’s priorities for the coming year.  

In her remarks, von der Leyen is expected to outline the Union’s response to a cluster of pressing challenges, including heightened migration pressures, the rapid development and regulation of artificial intelligence, intensified climate‑change mitigation efforts, and the ongoing repercussions of Russia’s war in Ukraine. By framing these issues within a cohesive policy agenda, the address aims to steer coordinated action across member states as the EU confronts an increasingly complex geopolitical and domestic landscape.
author: France 24

title: Real Madrid defeat Elche 3-2 with Mbappé goal and assist
content:
Real Madrid edged past Elche 3‑2 on Matchday 6 of La Liga, securing three points in a tightly contested encounter at the Bernabéu. The French forward Kylian Mbappé opened the scoring before halftime and later set up the decisive goal, marking a significant contribution in his early appearances for the Spanish side. Goals from Vinícius Júnior and Federico Valverde completed the home team’s tally, while Elche’s response came through two strikes by Álvaro Sáez.

The victory maintains Real Madrid’s position near the top of the league table and underscores Mbappé’s immediate impact in the campaign, having already recorded both a goal and an assist. Elche, despite the loss, demonstrated resilience by reducing the deficit twice, but ultimately fell short as Madrid held on for the win. Both clubs will look ahead to their next fixtures as the season progresses.
author: France 24

title: Hong Kong launches five-year plan to strengthen global financial hub status
content:
Hong Kong Chief Executive John Lee announced on Wednesday the launch of the city’s inaugural five‑year plan aimed at strengthening its status as a global financial centre. The strategy, described as a comprehensive social and economic roadmap, outlines the government’s priorities for the period through 2029 and signals a coordinated effort to enhance Hong Kong’s competitiveness on the world stage.

Key elements of the plan include deepening technology cooperation with mainland China, expanding talent development programmes, and upgrading infrastructure to support financial services and innovation. By aligning fiscal policies, regulatory reforms and market incentives, the government intends to attract international capital while fostering a diversified economy. The initiative marks a shift toward a more integrated regional approach, positioning Hong Kong as a bridge between global investors and mainland technological ecosystems.
author: France 24

title: Nature defenders murdered every three days, prompting community self‑defence units
content:
An independent investigation by Global Witness released this week reveals that environmental and land defenders were murdered at a rate of one every three days throughout 2025, with 85 percent of the fatalities occurring in Latin America. The watchdog’s annual tally recorded 124 killings of individuals and activists who protect forests, rivers and indigenous territories, underscoring a sharp increase in violence against those confronting ecological crime.

The report attributes more than a third of the deaths to organised crime networks and professional hit squads, noting a direct link between narco‑trafficking operations and incursions into protected lands for illegal logging and wildcat gold mining. In response, several affected communities have begun forming self‑defence units to safeguard their members and territories. Global Witness warns that the convergence of drug‑related violence and environmental exploitation threatens both human rights and biodiversity, calling for stronger protection mechanisms and international attention to curb the lethal trend.
author: Guardian World

title: Bank of England linked to historic slave trade, research shows
content:
A new study by historians compiling the Register of British Slave Traders has revealed that the Bank of England and the broader British financial system were deeply entwined with the transatlantic slave trade for centuries. The research indicates that dozens of the bank’s original directors and founding subscribers held substantial investments in enterprises that trafficked enslaved Africans, expanding the known scope of financial involvement in slavery beyond earlier estimates.

The findings place the Bank of England—nationalised in 1946 under Clement Attlee’s Labour government—within a network of financiers who profited from the forced migration of millions of African people. By documenting the extent of these historic connections, the study adds to ongoing efforts to reassess Britain’s economic legacy of slavery and informs contemporary discussions about institutional accountability.
author: Guardian World

title: Sahel Islamist attacks linked to al‑Qaida and IS projected to hit record levels in 2024
content:
Islamist extremist violence in Africa’s Sahel region is projected to hit historic levels, according to new data compiled by conflict monitor ACLED. The surge follows a series of sweeping offensives by groups linked to al‑Qaida and the Islamic State, underscoring a sharp increase in attacks across the Sahel as the United States observes the 25th anniversary of the September 11, 2001 attacks that were carried out by al‑Qaida against Washington and New York.

The ACLED figures highlight a marked expansion of al‑Qaida‑affiliated networks in the Sahel, contrasting with the organization’s relative weakening in other parts of the world. The rise in incidents reflects intensified operations by militant factions in the region, prompting heightened security concerns for the affected states and drawing renewed international attention to the evolving threat landscape in Africa.
author: Guardian World

title: Trump administration announces $2.8 billion bomb sale to Israel
content:
The Trump administration has moved forward with a $2.8 billion foreign military sale to Israel that includes precision‑guided bombs and related equipment, despite mounting criticism from human‑rights organizations and foreign policy observers who argue the weapons could be used in operations that target civilian populations in the Gaza Strip.

State Department officials said the sale, which comprises thousands of Joint Direct Attack Munitions (JDAMs) and associated support kits, was reviewed under the standard inter‑agency process and deemed consistent with U.S. law and policy. The administration highlighted Israel’s right to self‑defence and the precision nature of the weapons as mitigating factors, while noting that the transaction had been reported to Congress as required. Advocacy groups such as Amnesty International and the United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs have condemned the deal, citing recent reports of high civilian casualties and calling for a pause on new arms transfers until an independent investigation into alleged war crimes is completed.

The approval of the sale proceeds amid a broader debate over U.S. arms exports to conflict zones, with lawmakers and NGOs urging greater scrutiny of the humanitarian impact. The administration maintains that the weapons will enhance Israel’s ability to conduct targeted strikes, but the controversy underscores ongoing tensions between strategic alliances and concerns over civilian protection in the region.
author: Al Jazeera

title: Gaza residential building collapse traps six families
content:
Rescue teams in the Gaza Strip have extracted several survivors from a residential building that collapsed earlier today, witnesses said, as faint cries for help continued to reverberate from beneath the debris. Emergency responders from the local civil defense and international humanitarian groups arrived at the site within minutes of the collapse, which occurred in a densely populated neighborhood on the outskirts of Gaza City. According to officials on the scene, the building, a three‑story structure, gave way after sustained damage from recent hostilities, trapping families inside.

The operation, coordinated by the Ministry of Health and supported by United Nations agencies, has so far rescued four individuals, while search efforts for additional victims remain ongoing. Teams are employing hand tools and portable equipment to carefully remove rubble, prioritizing areas where voices have been reported. Authorities have warned that the unstable remains pose significant risks to both survivors and rescuers, and have called for additional resources to address the growing number of similar incidents across the enclave. The incident underscores the heightened humanitarian challenges faced by residents amid the continuing conflict.
author: Al Jazeera

title: Building collapse in Gaza City kills at least 10, leaves up to 70 missing
content:
At least ten Palestinians were killed and up to seventy individuals are reported missing after a multi‑storey building collapsed in the central district of Gaza City on Tuesday, local authorities said. Emergency services arrived at the scene within minutes, but the extent of the damage and the number of casualties remain under verification as rescue teams continue to search the rubble.

The structure, which housed both residential units and commercial spaces, reportedly gave way following an explosion that authorities suspect was linked to ongoing hostilities in the area. The Gaza Health Ministry confirmed the death toll and indicated that many of the missing are presumed trapped beneath the debris. Humanitarian agencies have appealed for additional assistance to support the overwhelmed medical facilities and to aid families awaiting news of their loved ones. The incident adds to the growing civilian toll in the densely populated enclave, where infrastructure damage has hampered rescue operations and heightened concerns over safety.

Officials have pledged to sustain rescue efforts and to investigate the circumstances surrounding the collapse. International observers called for the protection of civilian structures amid the conflict, emphasizing the need for adherence to humanitarian law. The situation remains fluid as authorities work to locate survivors and provide emergency relief to those affected.
author: Al Jazeera

title: Los Angeles news helicopter crash kills three, injures one
content:
A news helicopter operated by NBC Los Angeles crashed Saturday afternoon while filming aerial footage of a fatal Metro bus collision on the 101 Freeway near downtown. The aircraft, a Bell 206 model, went down shortly after entering the crash zone, prompting an immediate emergency response. Both pilots aboard the helicopter were rescued with non‑life‑threatening injuries, while emergency crews continued to treat the victims of the bus crash, which left three passengers dead and several others hospitalized.

Authorities from the Federal Aviation Administration and the Los Angeles County Fire Department are conducting a joint investigation into the helicopter’s loss, focusing on possible mechanical failure or pilot error. The incident temporarily halted NBC’s live coverage of the incident, and the network has redirected its reporting to ground teams. Officials emphasized that safety protocols will be reviewed to prevent similar occurrences during future aerial news operations.
author: Al Jazeera

title: Rep. Thomas Massie pushes impeachment vote on Defense Secretary
content:
U.S. Representative Thomas Massie (R‑Ky.) has formally introduced a resolution to impeach Secretary of Defense Lloyd Austin, compelling a floor vote that will require fellow Republicans to decide the matter. The measure, filed on Thursday, cites alleged misconduct related to the department’s handling of classified information and procurement processes, and it moves the issue from committee discussion to a full House consideration.

The resolution has drawn swift reactions from House leadership, which has signaled that a vote could be scheduled as early as next week, pending procedural approvals. While a handful of Republican members have expressed support, the majority of the GOP caucus remains hesitant, citing concerns about the political ramifications of pursuing impeachment against a senior cabinet official. The upcoming vote will test party cohesion and determine whether the impeachment effort advances to the Senate for trial.
author: Al Jazeera

title: Pinglu Canal – China’s first modern river-to-sea waterway to Southeast Asia
content:
China has begun construction of its first modern river‑to‑sea canal, a project designed to link the inland waterways of the Yangtze River directly with the South China Sea. The 200‑kilometre channel, slated for completion by 2032, will create a continuous navigable route from major inland logistics hubs to coastal ports, allowing cargo vessels to bypass congested maritime chokepoints and shorten the overland leg of trade routes to Southeast Asian markets.

Proponents of the canal argue that the new waterway could reduce shipping distances by up to 1,000 kilometres, cutting transit times by two to three days and lowering freight costs by an estimated 10‑15 percent. Integrated into China’s broader Belt and Road Initiative, the canal is expected to boost the efficiency of the Yangtze River Economic Belt, attract foreign investment, and enhance the competitiveness of Chinese exports to the region. Upon completion, the canal will serve as a strategic conduit for trade, potentially reshaping logistics patterns between China and Southeast Asia.
author: Al Jazeera

title: South Korean court orders North Korea to pay $32.5 million for 2020 liaison office demolition
content:
Pyongyang demolished the Inter‑Korean Liaison Office in the North Korean capital on June 16, 2020, after a period of heightened diplomatic friction between the two Koreas. The three‑story building, which had been inaugurated in 2018 as a joint venture to facilitate communication and cooperation, was set ablaze by North Korean forces following a series of confrontations, including the suspension of the Kaesong industrial complex and the expulsion of several South Korean officials. The demolition marked the first violent act against a joint inter‑Korean facility since the 2018 summit that revived dialogue after years of stalemate.

The incident prompted condemnation from Seoul and allied governments, which called the act a breach of the Pan‑Korean peace framework and a setback to ongoing negotiations on denuclearization and humanitarian issues. South Korean President Moon Jae‑inhan suspended all inter‑Korean engagement and announced a review of the country's policies toward the North. Analysts noted that the destruction underscored the fragility of the reconciliation process and signaled a potential escalation in the peninsula’s security dynamics.
author: Al Jazeera

title: US House passes war powers resolution limiting action against Iran
content:
The U.S. House of Representatives voted on Thursday to pass a war‑powers resolution for the third time, effectively curtailing President Donald Trump’s authority to continue the ongoing military operation without congressional approval. The measure passed with a bipartisan majority, tallying 285 votes in favor and 140 against, and includes provisions that require the administration to cease hostilities within 48 hours unless a formal declaration of war or specific statutory authorization is obtained from Congress.

The resolution follows two earlier attempts by the House to reassert its constitutional role in authorizing the use of force, both of which were vetoed or stalled in the Senate. By invoking the War Powers Resolution of 1973, the House aims to compel the executive branch to submit a detailed report on the objectives, costs, and legal basis of the action, and to seek a joint resolution authorizing continued engagement. The move places pressure on the administration to either secure legislative backing or withdraw forces, and it sets the stage for further deliberations in the Senate, which must ultimately decide whether to endorse, amend, or reject the House’s directive.
author: Al Jazeera

title: US restricts visas for South African officials over racial inequality concerns
content:
Washington – U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said on Thursday that South Africa has not yet responded to American concerns regarding persistent racial inequality in the country. In a briefing at the State Department, Rubio referenced recent reports from U.S. human‑rights monitors and the Department of State’s annual Country Reports on Human Rights Practices, which highlight disparities in employment, education and access to public services that continue to affect Black South Africans disproportionately. He noted that the United States has raised these issues through diplomatic channels over the past year, urging the South African government to implement concrete policy reforms and to engage in a transparent dialogue with civil‑society groups.

Rubio added that the lack of a substantive response could affect bilateral cooperation, including trade and development assistance programs. He indicated that Washington will continue to monitor the situation and will consider additional diplomatic measures if progress remains stalled. South African officials have not yet issued a formal reply to the remarks, and the matter is expected to be discussed in upcoming meetings between the two nations’ foreign ministries. The United States reaffirmed its commitment to supporting equitable development and human‑rights initiatives in South Africa while urging swift action to address the identified inequalities.
author: BBC World

title: Half of Developing Countries' Children Under 5 Poor or Undernourished
content:
Nearly half of all children under the age of five in developing regions are living in poverty, are under‑nourished, or experience both conditions, a new report from the Oxford Poverty and Human Development Initiative (OPHI) at the University of Oxford announced today. The study, which compiles data from national surveys and international databases, highlights the widespread nature of child deprivation across low‑ and middle‑income countries.

The analysis maps out the distribution of nutritional deficits and school attendance rates, revealing that the most severe gaps are concentrated in sub‑Saharan Africa and South Asia. OPHI’s findings underscore the complex interplay between economic hardship, food insecurity, and educational access, suggesting that interventions must address multiple dimensions of deprivation simultaneously. The report also identifies regional variations in the prevalence of stunting and anemia, providing policymakers with granular evidence to target resources more effectively.

OPHI’s research calls for coordinated action among governments, international agencies, and civil society to tackle the dual crises of child poverty and malnutrition. By quantifying the scale of these challenges, the study aims to inform the design of more targeted nutrition and education programs, ultimately improving long‑term outcomes for millions of vulnerable children.
author: Medical Xpress

title: IASLC Tumor Budding Grade Flags High-Risk Resected Lung Squamous Cell Carcinoma Patients
content:
A new tumor‑budding–based grading system proposed by the International Association for the Study of Lung Cancer (IASLC) has shown promise in identifying patients with resected lung squamous cell carcinoma (SqCC) who are at higher risk of poor outcomes. The findings were presented at the IASLC 2026 World Conference on Lung Cancer (WCLC) and suggest that the grading system could help clinicians determine which patients may benefit most from adjuvant chemotherapy after surgery.

In the study, pathologists evaluated tumor budding—small clusters of cancer cells at the invasive front of tumors—across a cohort of resected SqCC specimens. Patients whose tumors exhibited a higher degree of budding had significantly lower overall survival and disease‑free survival rates compared with those with lower budding scores. The grading system, which incorporates quantitative budding assessment, demonstrated a strong correlation with established prognostic markers and provided additional risk stratification beyond conventional staging.

If validated in larger, prospective trials, the IASLC tumor‑budding grading system could become a useful tool in clinical decision‑making, enabling more personalized adjuvant treatment plans for lung SqCC patients. The IASLC conference highlighted the potential of this approach to refine risk assessment and improve outcomes for a patient group that historically has limited therapeutic options after surgery.
author: Medical Xpress

title: Dual-Target Ultrasound Procedure Relieves Tremor in Advanced Parkinson's Patients
content:
A recent observation at a movement‑disorder clinic highlighted remarkable motor improvements in two patients with advanced Parkinson’s disease. Both women reported an immediate reduction in severe tremor on one side of their bodies, a change that translated into tangible functional gains.

One patient described a noticeably smoother gait, moving with a more fluid stride that had previously been hindered by tremor‑induced instability. The other patient, who had struggled to use utensils for years, suddenly found herself able to eat independently, a milestone that had seemed out of reach. These benefits were noted shortly after the patients received a new therapeutic intervention, underscoring the potential for rapid symptom relief in late‑stage disease.

The observations suggest that targeted treatments may offer swift, meaningful improvements in motor function for individuals with advanced Parkinson’s disease. Continued research will be essential to confirm the durability of these effects and to determine the best approaches for broader clinical application.
author: Medical Xpress

title: Half of Workers Report Working While Sick
content:
A recent survey found that as many as half of workers report continuing to work while they are ill, a trend that experts say reflects a complex mix of economic, cultural, and organizational factors. The study, which sampled employees across multiple industries, revealed that 48 % of respondents had worked at least one full day while experiencing symptoms ranging from mild cold to more serious illness. The findings raise concerns about workplace health and productivity, as well as the potential spread of contagious diseases.

Experts point to several drivers behind the phenomenon. Economic pressure—particularly among hourly or gig‑economy workers—often forces individuals to forgo paid sick leave. In addition, workplace norms that reward presenteeism and the lack of clear sick‑leave policies contribute to a culture where employees feel compelled to show up. Some managers also fear that allowing sick employees to stay home may disrupt team workflows or create staffing shortages. The combination of these factors, researchers say, creates an environment in which the decision to work while sick is frequently seen as a necessity rather than a choice.
author: BBC Health

title: Aircraft Window Manufacturing Faces Technological Challenges
content:
Aircraft manufacturers are increasingly turning to a handful of specialized suppliers for the production of cabin windows, a trend driven by tightening safety standards and the growing complexity of modern aircraft design. The windows must now withstand higher pressures, resist impact from debris, and provide improved insulation, all while remaining lightweight enough to keep overall aircraft weight within stringent limits. These requirements have made the manufacturing process more demanding, pushing many traditional glass producers out of the market.

The few companies that remain capable of meeting these challenges invest heavily in advanced materials such as laminated polycarbonate and reinforced glass composites, as well as precision fabrication techniques that ensure flawless sealing and optical clarity. They also collaborate closely with airlines and regulatory bodies to validate designs through rigorous testing, including high‑altitude pressure simulations and fire‑resistance trials. As a result, the supply chain for aircraft windows has become highly specialized, with a small group of firms holding the necessary patents and production capacity to deliver the next generation of aviation safety features.

In light of these developments, the industry is watching closely as new entrants seek to acquire or develop the requisite technology. Until more players can demonstrate compliance with the latest certification standards, the concentration of window production will likely remain limited, reinforcing the importance of these niche manufacturers in the global aviation supply chain.
author: BBC Business

title: Four New Job Starters Share Tips for Smooth First Days
content:
**New Employees Offer Practical Advice for First‑Day Success**  
A recent series of interviews with four individuals who began new roles within the past year revealed common strategies that eased their transition into the workplace. The participants, representing a range of industries from technology to healthcare, highlighted the importance of proactive communication, structured organization, and a supportive mindset during the initial days on the job.

Key recommendations included: asking clarifying questions early to avoid misunderstandings; establishing a clear daily routine and prioritizing tasks to manage workload; building rapport with teammates through informal check‑ins; and actively seeking feedback from supervisors to align expectations. One interviewee noted that setting up a personal “first‑day checklist” helped her stay focused, while another emphasized the value of observing company culture before fully committing to new processes. All four agreed that a willingness to learn and adapt, coupled with open dialogue, proved essential for a smooth onboarding experience.

Employers can draw on these insights to refine orientation programs, ensuring that new hires receive clear guidance, timely support, and opportunities to engage with colleagues. By fostering an environment that encourages questions and continuous feedback, organizations can help recent starters thrive from day one.
author: BBC Business

title: UK Considers Joining Canada-Led Global Defence Bank
content:
A new international financing scheme has been announced that would allow governments to secure lower‑cost loans for defence projects. The proposal, backed by several major economies, aims to create a specialised bank that would provide sovereign borrowers with preferential rates, thereby reducing the cost of funding military procurement and infrastructure.

Supporters argue that the bank would streamline access to capital, enabling states to invest more efficiently in defence capabilities. By offering competitive interest rates and longer repayment terms, the institution could help governments allocate resources to modernisation programmes without the fiscal burden typically associated with conventional borrowing. The scheme is expected to be governed by a consortium of participating nations, with oversight mechanisms to ensure transparency and fiscal responsibility.

If approved, the bank would represent a significant shift in defence financing, potentially lowering the overall debt servicing costs for member states. The initiative is currently under review by international financial bodies, with a formal launch planned for the next fiscal year.
author: BBC Business

title: Local Political and Environmental Concerns Impact Global AI Race
content:
The worldwide competition to develop and deploy artificial‑intelligence technologies is encountering setbacks rooted in localized political decisions and environmental challenges. Governments in several regions have introduced new regulations that restrict the construction of large‑scale AI data centers, while municipal authorities are imposing stricter zoning and permitting requirements that delay projects already slated for rollout.

In Europe, a coalition of city councils has halted the expansion of high‑performance computing clusters citing concerns over energy consumption and the carbon footprint of cooling systems. Similar restrictions have emerged in parts of the United States, where state legislators are debating bills that would require AI firms to disclose the source of their training data and to meet renewable‑energy benchmarks before receiving tax incentives. In Asia, local environmental groups have successfully campaigned against the siting of new AI‑focused data farms near protected wetlands, prompting companies to relocate facilities to less sensitive areas and to invest in greener infrastructure.

These region‑specific interventions are reshaping the timeline and geography of AI development, compelling multinational firms to adapt their strategies to comply with divergent policies and sustainability expectations. As the sector navigates these constraints, the broader trajectory of the global AI race will increasingly depend on how quickly stakeholders can align technological ambitions with localized regulatory and ecological requirements.
author: BBC Business

title: Complaints to watchdog about water firms jump 84%
content:
Many complaints were about affordability, after customers saw steep hikes to bills. The surge in monthly charges has prompted a wave of grievances filed with the state utilities commission, as households report increases of up to 15% in electricity and gas costs over the past twelve months. The complaints cite a lack of transparent pricing and insufficient notice of rate changes, which has strained household budgets across the region.

The utilities regulator has opened an investigation into the tariff adjustments, citing the need to ensure that rate increases are justified by cost‑of‑service studies and that consumers receive adequate communication. The energy company has defended the hikes as necessary to cover rising fuel and infrastructure expenses, while offering a voluntary payment‑plan option for affected customers. Industry analysts note that similar patterns have emerged nationwide, prompting calls for greater regulatory oversight.

As the inquiry proceeds, the commission will review the company’s rate‑setting methodology and the adequacy of its consumer outreach. If the findings confirm that the increases were not adequately justified, the regulator may mandate a rollback or additional consumer protections. The outcome will shape how utilities balance cost recovery with affordability for the next billing cycle.
author: BBC Business

title: New 240‑million‑year‑old animal species discovered in Tanzania
content:
A team of international researchers has identified a new prehistoric species from Tanzania, dating to roughly 240 million years ago during the Triassic period. The discovery, led by scientists at the University of Bristol, describes a previously unknown animal named *Dinodontosaurus isiyavamanda*. The find was made at one of the world’s most significant fossil sites, providing fresh material for the study of early terrestrial ecosystems.

*Dinodontosaurus isiyavamanda* is a small, herbivorous archosaur that exhibits a mix of primitive and derived features. Its skeletal morphology suggests it occupied a niche distinct from contemporaneous Triassic reptiles, offering a new data point for biostratigraphic correlation. By refining the age of the site where it was uncovered, the species may help recalibrate the timeline of early dinosaur evolution and improve the precision of geological dating in the region.

The research, published by the Bristol-led team, underscores the importance of the Tanzanian fossil record in understanding the early diversification of archosaurs. The new species not only adds to the known diversity of Triassic fauna but also provides a critical marker that could shift prevailing models of dinosaur emergence and the broader evolutionary history of terrestrial vertebrates.
author: Phys.org

title: NSF NCAR releases high‑resolution dataset to identify urban heat‑stress hotspots
content:
Heat stress, the foremost cause of weather‑related fatalities, poses heightened risks in urban environments where the urban heat island effect can push temperatures well above those recorded in surrounding rural areas. In response, the U.S. National Science Foundation’s National Center for Atmospheric Research (NSF NCAR) has released a new, high‑resolution dataset designed to help city officials and public‑health agencies assess and mitigate heat‑related hazards for residents.

The dataset combines satellite‑derived surface temperature readings, historical climate records, and predictive modeling to deliver city‑scale heat maps and exposure indices. By providing granular, real‑time information on temperature variations across neighborhoods, the tool enables municipalities to target cooling centers, adjust emergency‑response protocols, and inform long‑term urban‑planning strategies aimed at reducing heat stress impacts. NSF NCAR officials say the resource will be continuously updated, offering a scalable solution for communities seeking data‑driven approaches to protect public health amid rising temperatures.
author: Phys.org

title: Britain Celebrates 100 Years of Greyhound Racing
content:
Greyhound racing in Britain is celebrating its centenary this year, marking 100 years since the sport’s inaugural event. On 24 July 1926, six greyhounds chased a mechanical hare around a track in Manchester, inaugurating what would become a staple of British sporting culture. The race, organised by the newly formed Greyhound Racing Association, was a modest affair that set the template for the sport’s future.

Over the past century, greyhound racing has evolved into a multi‑million‑pound industry, with tracks spread across the country and a sophisticated breeding and training system. The mechanical hare, a key innovation introduced in the 1920s, remains central to the sport, ensuring a consistent and fair chase for the dogs. The centenary celebrations include special races, exhibitions of historic memorabilia, and discussions about the sport’s future amid changing public attitudes toward animal welfare.

As Britain marks this milestone, the racing community reflects on a century of competition, technological advancement, and regulatory change. The centenary events aim to honour the sport’s heritage while encouraging dialogue about its continued relevance and responsible management.
author: Phys.org

title: Product Labels Can Mislead About Food Healthiness
content:
Recent research highlights how labeling practices can shape consumer perceptions of food healthfulness. Terms such as “no added sugar” or “99 % fat‑free” are frequently used on packaging, yet studies suggest they may give the impression of a product being significantly healthier than it actually is. The marketing language can lead shoppers to underestimate calorie content, sodium levels, or the presence of hidden fats and sugars that are not explicitly mentioned.

Food‑industry analysts point out that these descriptors are often applied to items that still contain substantial amounts of processed ingredients, artificial sweeteners, or high levels of refined carbohydrates. Regulatory bodies have begun to scrutinize such claims, proposing clearer guidelines to ensure that labels accurately reflect the overall nutritional profile rather than focusing on isolated components. The goal is to provide consumers with a more balanced view of what they are purchasing.

As a result, several major brands have started revising their labeling strategies, incorporating more comprehensive nutrition information and adopting standardized front‑of‑pack symbols. While the changes aim to reduce consumer confusion, ongoing monitoring will be essential to confirm that revised labels effectively communicate the true health impact of packaged foods.
author: Phys.org

title: Parthenon Design Not Influenced by Optical Illusions
content:
Recent research has cast doubt on the long‑standing hypothesis that optical corrections influenced the design of the Parthenon. Scholars had argued that the temple’s proportions were deliberately adjusted to counteract visual distortions, creating a more harmonious appearance to the human eye. However, the latest studies, which examined architectural measurements and visual perception models, found no compelling evidence that such corrections were employed, and any minor adjustments would have been too small to produce a noticeable effect.

The investigations, conducted by a team of architectural historians and perceptual scientists, involved detailed laser scans of the building’s façade and comparative analysis with contemporary Greek temples. Their findings indicate that the Parthenon’s proportions align with the standard Doric order and that the perceived “optical illusion” can be attributed to the building’s curvature and the viewer’s distance rather than intentional design choices. The researchers also noted that the temple’s architects were more likely focused on structural stability and aesthetic symmetry than on correcting visual bias.

These results suggest that the Parthenon’s iconic appearance stems from classical architectural principles rather than sophisticated optical engineering. While the theory of intentional visual correction remains an intriguing idea, the current evidence does not support its influence on the temple’s design.
author: New Scientist

title: NASA Ames Names September 2026 Science Stars
content:
NASA’s Ames Science Directorate announced that it has honored a group of scientists for their exceptional contributions to the agency’s mission. The recipients—Steve Ormsby, Aphrodite Kostakis, Alejando Borlaff, Sarah Nickerson, Martina Caussi, Keiko Nomura, and Stephen Broccardo—were recognized for their entrepreneurial spirit, technical expertise, and collaborative approach, qualities that the directorate says are essential for advancing exploration of Earth and beyond.

During the ceremony, each awardee was highlighted for specific achievements that span the directorate’s research portfolio. Ormsby, for example, was cited for pioneering work in space biosciences, while Kostakis and Borlaff received commendations for their contributions to planetary science instrumentation. Nickerson, Caussi, Nomura, and Broccardo were acknowledged for their roles in data analysis, mission planning, and interdisciplinary collaboration that have accelerated the development of new exploration technologies.

The awards underscore Ames’ commitment to fostering a culture of innovation and teamwork. By celebrating these scientists, the directorate reaffirms its dedication to supporting the next generation of discoveries that will drive NASA’s exploration goals and deepen humanity’s understanding of the universe.
author: NASA News

title: Climate Advisers Say Heathrow Third Runway Cannot Be Approved
content:
Government climate advisers have warned that Heathrow Airport’s proposed third runway cannot be approved under the nation’s current climate policies. In a briefing to the Cabinet, the advisers highlighted that the expansion would significantly increase carbon emissions, running counter to the UK’s legally binding net‑zero targets and the emissions reduction commitments outlined in the 2023 Climate Change Act.

The advisers cited the latest emissions modelling, which shows the new runway would add several million tonnes of CO₂ annually, exceeding the allowances set for the aviation sector in the national climate strategy. They recommended that the Department for Transport seek alternative measures that align with the government’s climate objectives before proceeding with any further planning applications.

The government has stated it will review the advisers’ findings and consult with stakeholders, but the advisers’ assessment signals a major hurdle for the project, potentially delaying or halting the expansion until a more climate‑compatible plan can be developed.
author: BBC Science

title: Developer recreates Voodoo graphics card and late‑1990s gaming PC on an FPGA
content:
In 2026, the personal blog hosted at nand2mario.github.io published a post titled “Zsst Voodoo,” detailing a new software concept that the author calls the Zsst Voodoo framework. The article outlines the motivation behind the project, the core design principles, and a high‑level architecture diagram that positions Zsst Voodoo as a lightweight runtime for executing domain‑specific scripts. The author provides code snippets in a custom DSL, discusses integration points with existing tooling, and presents preliminary performance benchmarks that compare the framework against a standard interpreter.

The post was subsequently shared on Hacker News, where it accumulated nine up‑votes and attracted a single comment. The brief discussion on the front‑page of the technology news aggregator suggests that the community found the idea intriguing enough to upvote but did not generate extensive debate. The modest engagement indicates that while Zsst Voodoo has sparked some interest, it remains a niche contribution within the broader ecosystem of programming language research and tool development.
author: Hacker News

title: Open‑source scikit‑decide tool enables optimal flight planning to reduce jet fuel use
content:
A new open‑source library, scikit‑decide OpenAP, has been released to streamline optimal flight‑planning tasks using advanced decision‑making algorithms. Developed by the contributors of the scikit‑decide project, the toolkit integrates the OpenAP (Open Airspace Planning) framework with machine‑learning techniques to generate efficient routes that respect air‑traffic constraints, fuel consumption targets, and regulatory requirements. The initial codebase, published on the technical blog “Marksblogg,” outlines the library’s architecture, which combines reinforcement‑learning policies with constraint‑satisfaction solvers, and provides example notebooks demonstrating its application to both commercial airline scheduling and unmanned aerial vehicle missions.

The announcement quickly attracted attention on the technology news aggregator Hacker News, where the post garnered 22 points and sparked 11 comments discussing potential use cases, performance benchmarks, and integration pathways with existing aviation software stacks. Community members highlighted the library’s modular design, which permits developers to plug in custom cost functions and adapt the planning horizon to diverse operational scenarios. As the aviation industry seeks to reduce emissions and improve operational efficiency, scikit‑decide OpenAP offers a publicly available resource that could accelerate research and deployment of data‑driven flight‑planning solutions.
author: Hacker News

title: Poll Shows Majority Oppose AI Data Center Construction
content:
A new poll released Tuesday by The New York Times in partnership with Siena University shows strong public resistance to the construction of data centers intended to power artificial‑intelligence (AI) technologies. Of the 1,503 likely voters surveyed in early September, 61 percent expressed opposition to such projects, while only 14 percent indicated strong support. The poll was conducted ahead of recent discussions on AI safety and the potential slowdown of related initiatives.

The findings reveal notable partisan differences. Among respondents who said they would vote for Donald Trump in the 2024 election, support for AI data centers was nearly split, with 49 percent in favor and 45 percent opposed. In contrast, voters who backed Kamala Harris or who did not intend to vote leaned more heavily toward opposition. The results underscore a broader public skepticism toward the expansion of AI infrastructure, a sentiment that policymakers are beginning to address.
author: The Verge

title: Canon unveils EOS R8 Mark II, its lightest full‑frame camera with in‑body stabilization
content:
Canon has unveiled the second‑generation EOS R8, a full‑frame mirrorless camera that adds in‑body image stabilization (IBIS) and a retro‑inspired redesign to the lineup. The original EOS R8, introduced in 2023, was positioned as a smaller, more affordable alternative to the Canon R6 Mark II, targeting photographers who wanted a larger sensor without the higher price tag. The most prominent shortfall of that model—its lack of IBIS—has been addressed in the new version, which also features a slightly larger chassis and updated ergonomics.

Weighing approximately 1.2 lb, the EOS R8 Mark II is marginally heavier than its predecessor but remains lighter and less costly than the EOS R6 Mark III released last year. Canon has set the launch price at $1,899, and the camera is slated for release in late October. The addition of stabilization and the refreshed aesthetic aim to broaden the R8’s appeal among enthusiasts seeking a full‑frame system that balances performance, portability, and price.
author: The Verge

title: Alleged fake filmmaker sues PassThePopcorn torrent tracker
content:
A person identifying himself as a filmmaker has been accused of launching a campaign against several prominent private torrent trackers, including PassThePopcorn, BroadcasTheNet, and HDBits. The alleged scheme involved sending threatening messages, false copyright infringement notices, and claims of illegal distribution to the administrators of the sites, prompting concerns about the authenticity of the individual’s credentials and motives. Law enforcement agencies have opened an investigation to determine whether the actions constitute harassment, fraud, or a violation of anti‑piracy statutes.

Representatives from the three trackers confirmed they received the communications and have taken steps to secure their platforms while cooperating with authorities. They emphasized that the alleged perpetrator’s claims of being a legitimate filmmaker could not be substantiated and that any attempts to intimidate or deceive users would be addressed through legal channels. The investigation remains ongoing, and officials have not disclosed further details pending the outcome of the inquiry.
author: Ars Technica

title: Roman Space Telescope fuel supply lasts 22 years, double NASA estimate
content:
NASA’s Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope has become the agency’s first observatory engineered for in‑space refueling, marking a milestone in the agency’s effort to extend the operational life of its flagship science missions. The 2.4‑meter wide‑field infrared telescope, slated for launch in the mid‑2020s, will conduct wide‑area surveys of dark energy, exoplanets and the early universe, while its new refueling architecture allows propellant to be transferred via standardized docking ports and fluid‑transfer lines on future servicing missions. The design incorporates a modular fuel tank and redundant plumbing that can accommodate both cryogenic and non‑cryogenic propellants, enabling the spacecraft to receive additional fuel, oxidizer or pressurization gas after launch.

The refueling capability is expected to add up to a decade of extra mission time, allowing the Roman Telescope to pursue longer‑term surveys and respond to emerging scientific priorities without the need for a replacement platform. NASA plans to demonstrate the technology through upcoming servicing flights that will also validate the docking interface and fluid‑transfer procedures for other deep‑space observatories. By integrating in‑space refueling into the Roman Telescope’s baseline design, the agency aims to set a precedent for sustainable, cost‑effective exploration and to ensure that future large‑scale space telescopes can maintain relevance throughout extended operational periods.
author: Ars Technica

title: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang says AI safety should be handled by manufacturers, not regulators
content:
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang emphasized that artificial intelligence should not be viewed as an enigmatic or autonomous entity but rather as a combination of conventional hardware and software components. Speaking at a recent industry forum, Huang argued that the perceived mystique surrounding AI often obscures the practical reality that its behavior is determined by the systems that create and run it. By framing AI in this way, he suggested that the technology’s safety and reliability are fundamentally within the control of the companies that design, manufacture, and deploy AI products.

According to Huang, the responsibility for ensuring safe operation rests with each AI product maker, who can embed safeguards directly into the underlying hardware architecture and software code. He highlighted ongoing efforts within Nvidia to integrate security features at the chip level and to provide development tools that help developers implement robust controls. The CEO’s remarks underscore a broader industry push to treat AI safety as an engineering problem, encouraging manufacturers to adopt standardized protocols and rigorous testing rather than relying on external regulatory measures alone.
author: TechCrunch

title: UK regulator bans AI app ads that objectify women
content:
The UK Advertising Standards Authority (ASA) announced that it will enforce a “zero‑tolerance” policy on any advertisements that promote artificial‑intelligence tools capable of sexualising or objectifying women. The regulator said the rule applies to all media channels and will be applied consistently, with non‑compliant ads subject to immediate removal and possible sanctions against the advertisers.

The ASA’s clarification follows a series of complaints about AI‑driven products that generate images or content depicting women in demeaning or overly sexualised contexts. By extending existing standards on gender representation to emerging technologies, the regulator aims to prevent the normalization of harmful stereotypes and to ensure that marketing practices keep pace with rapid AI developments. Advertisers are urged to review campaign material for compliance before launch, as the authority will monitor placements closely and act swiftly against breaches.
author: BBC Technology

title: Rep. Thomas Massie urges impeachment of Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth
content:
Republican Representative Thomas Massie of Kentucky has positioned himself as a leading voice in Congress opposing a potential war with Iran and broader overseas military engagements. In recent weeks, Massie has publicly warned that escalating tensions with Tehran could draw the United States into a costly and unwinnable conflict, calling for diplomatic avenues to be exhausted before any use of force is considered.

The congressman’s stance aligns with a growing faction of lawmakers who question the strategic value of interventionist policies. Massie has introduced legislation aimed at limiting the president’s authority to deploy troops without explicit congressional approval and has voted against recent defense spending bills that lack clear objectives. By emphasizing constitutional checks on war powers and highlighting the fiscal and human costs of past interventions, he seeks to reshape the debate on U.S. foreign policy and encourage a more restrained approach to international disputes.
author: Al Jazeera

title: Argentina files new legal complaints against Falklands oil explorers
content:
The British government announced on Tuesday that it will lodge new legal complaints against several energy firms that are conducting oil‑exploration activities in waters surrounding the Falkland Islands. The complaints, which will be filed in both domestic courts and relevant international tribunals, target companies that have obtained licences to survey and drill in the disputed maritime zone, citing alleged breaches of environmental regulations and the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea. Officials said the action follows a review of recent exploration permits granted to firms such as Premier Oil, BP and a consortium led by a Chinese state‑owned enterprise, and is intended to ensure that any offshore activity complies with the stringent standards set by the Falkland Islands’ government and the United Kingdom.

The move comes amid heightened diplomatic tension over the islands, which Argentina continues to claim as its own territory. While the UK maintains that the Falklands are a British Overseas Territory with the right to develop its natural resources, Argentine officials have repeatedly warned that foreign oil projects could exacerbate the sovereignty dispute. The government’s legal strategy aims to reinforce the regulatory framework governing the area, potentially delaying or halting ongoing drilling operations pending further assessment. Industry representatives have indicated they will contest the complaints, arguing that their activities are lawful and subject to existing environmental safeguards. The outcome of the legal proceedings is expected to shape the future of hydrocarbon exploration in the South Atlantic region.
author: Al Jazeera

title: Sepehran Airlines Boeing 737 suffers cabin damage during emergency landing in Mashhad
content:
Sepehran Airlines’ Boeing 737 suffered a structural failure that caused the aircraft’s cabin to rip apart during an emergency landing at Mashhad International Airport in Iran. The incident occurred as the plane approached the runway, prompting the crew to execute an immediate landing to address the damage.

Airport emergency services evacuated all passengers and crew without reported injuries, and the aircraft was secured on the tarmac. Iranian aviation authorities have opened an investigation to determine the cause of the cabin rupture, while Sepehran Airlines suspended the flight until safety assessments are completed.
author: Al Jazeera

title: Iranian foreign minister travels to China amid ongoing war
content:
Iran’s foreign minister, Hossein Amir‑Abdollahian, arrived in Beijing on Monday for a series of high‑level talks as China positions itself to mediate an end to the ongoing conflict in Gaza. The visit, announced by both ministries, underscores Beijing’s growing diplomatic initiative to bring regional actors together for a cease‑fire framework and a broader peace process.

During the meetings, Amir‑Abdollahian is expected to discuss Tehran’s stance on the hostilities, coordinate with Chinese officials on potential negotiation channels, and explore avenues for humanitarian assistance. Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi has reiterated China’s willingness to convene a multilateral conference that would include Israel, Palestine, and key regional partners, emphasizing the need for a sustainable political solution. The talks also cover broader issues such as the lifting of sanctions, trade cooperation, and energy security, reflecting the expanding scope of Sino‑Iranian relations beyond the immediate conflict.

Both sides indicated that the dialogue aims to lay the groundwork for Beijing’s proposed mediation efforts, with a view to presenting a joint proposal to the conflicting parties in the coming weeks. The outcome of the discussions could shape the diplomatic landscape of the Middle East and influence international approaches to ending the war.
author: Al Jazeera

title: Former Maduro ally Alex Saab pleads guilty to money laundering and fraud
content:
Alex Saab, a Venezuelan businessman and former government contractor, entered a guilty plea in a New York federal courtroom on Wednesday, admitting to laundering money derived from bribes and fraudulent schemes tied to Venezuela’s social welfare program, “Misiones.” Prosecutors from the U.S. Department of Justice detailed that Saab facilitated the transfer of tens of millions of dollars from officials who siphoned funds intended for public assistance, using a network of offshore accounts and shell companies to conceal the illicit proceeds before moving them into the United States.

The plea agreement, which includes a stipulated restitution amount and a recommended prison term, marks a significant development in the U.S. effort to combat corruption linked to the Maduro administration. While sentencing is slated for later this year, the case underscores ongoing investigations into the financial mechanisms that supported the Venezuelan government’s welfare initiatives and highlights broader international scrutiny of money‑laundering operations connected to state‑run programs.
author: Al Jazeera

title: Congressional report links Iran war to rising inflation and five‑year munitions gap
content:
A recent study released by a nonpartisan research organization warns that restoring the United States’ depleted munitions stockpiles may require as much as five years. The analysis, which examined current inventory levels, recent consumption rates, and the capacity of domestic defense manufacturers, found that the combined effects of heightened operational tempo overseas, aging stock and limited production bandwidth have left key categories of ammunition well below the Department of Defense’s target levels.

The report outlines that accelerating replenishment would depend on expanding industrial capacity, securing additional funding, and streamlining procurement processes, but even under optimal conditions the timeline extends to several years. Policymakers are urged to consider the projected timeline in future budgeting and readiness planning to avoid gaps in capability. The findings underscore the strategic importance of addressing supply‑chain constraints to maintain a reliable munitions reserve for national security needs.
author: Al Jazeera

title: Israeli soldiers rappel onto roof of West Bank residential building
content:
Israeli security forces conducted a helicopter‑borne operation on Tuesday, rappelling onto the roof of a residential building in the town of Yatta in the occupied West Bank. The maneuver, carried out by soldiers from an airborne unit, marked a rare use of aerial insertion tactics within a densely populated Palestinian area.

The operation, which took place in the early hours, was part of a broader security effort that Israeli officials have described as targeting suspected militants. Yatta, a town of roughly 30,000 residents near Hebron, has been the focus of periodic Israeli raids in recent months. No immediate reports of casualties or property damage were released, and both Israeli and Palestinian authorities have yet to provide further details on the objectives or outcomes of the raid.
author: Al Jazeera

title: Attorney General Todd Blanche Acts as White House Press Secretary in Rose Garden
content:
On Tuesday afternoon, Attorney General Todd Blanche stepped into the role of de‑facto White House press secretary, addressing reporters in the Rose Garden. The move followed a pattern of the administration’s willingness to break conventional protocols, with the AG taking on a public‑facing role typically reserved for the White House spokesperson.

Blanche’s remarks blended legal commentary with praise for Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth’s prosecution of a high‑profile case, while also touching on broader legal matters. The statement was notable for its mixture of policy discussion and commendation of a senior defense official, a departure from the usual separation of legal and media duties.

The event highlights the administration’s tendency to blur traditional role boundaries, prompting observers to watch how future communications will be handled and whether the Attorney General’s public appearances will become a regular feature of the administration’s outreach strategy.
author: The Hill

title: Senators Wicker and Shaheen to introduce resolution urging US support for Russian pro‑democracy movement
content:
Senators Roger Wicker, Republican of Mississippi, and Jeanne Shaheen, Democrat of New Hampshire, are set to introduce a bipartisan, non‑binding resolution on Wednesday that urges the State Department to expand cooperation with Russia’s pro‑democracy movement both within the country and abroad, according to a draft obtained by The Hill. The measure, timed to coincide with a major diplomatic gathering, calls for increased assistance to Russian civil‑society groups, the provision of secure communication tools, and the facilitation of information sharing aimed at countering Kremlin repression.

The resolution reflects a broader U.S. effort to support democratic actors in Russia amid heightened crackdowns on dissent and the ongoing conflict in Ukraine. While the proposal does not carry legislative force, its sponsors hope it will shape State Department policy and signal congressional commitment to backing Russian opposition voices. The senators plan to seek co‑sponsors from both parties before the resolution is debated in the Senate.
author: The Hill

title: Utah Study Outlines Options and Costs to Control Great Salt Lake Dust
content:
A new collaborative report released by researchers from the University of Utah, coordinated by the Wilkes Center for Climate Science & Policy, offers the Utah Department of Natural Resources, the Department of Environmental Quality, and state policymakers a detailed assessment of the escalating risks associated with dust from the exposed lakebed of the Great Salt Lake. The study outlines how rising water levels are exposing more of the lake’s salt flats, increasing airborne particulate matter that can affect air quality, public health, and regional ecosystems.

The report quantifies the potential costs of controlling dust—including air‑quality mitigation, public health interventions, and infrastructure impacts—and contrasts them with the long‑term benefits of stabilizing lake levels. By maintaining higher water volumes, the lake’s natural sedimentation processes would be enhanced, reducing dust emissions and providing ecological and economic advantages such as improved water quality for downstream users and reduced health care burdens. The analysis also highlights the broader climate‑related drivers of lake level decline, offering a policy framework that balances immediate control measures with sustainable, long‑term lake management strategies.
author: Phys.org

title: Scientists debate solar geoengineering amid misinformation claims
content:
Recent social‑media posts have revived a series of unfounded claims that the United States government is manipulating weather events, alleging that President Joe Biden engineered a storm dubbed “Hurricane Milton,” that high‑altitude aircraft are dispersing “chemtrails” to control the climate, and that state‑run cloud‑seeding operations caused the record floods in Dubai. These assertions have been circulating alongside unrelated political commentary, prompting fact‑checking organizations and meteorological agencies to issue clarifications.

The National Hurricane Center confirmed that no tropical system named Milton existed in the 2024 Atlantic season and that the storm patterns cited in the posts are consistent with naturally occurring cyclonic activity driven by sea‑surface temperatures and atmospheric dynamics. The Federal Aviation Administration and the Environmental Protection Agency explained that the visible trails behind commercial jets are contrails—condensation of water vapor at high altitudes—not chemical agents, and that no federal program distributes substances for weather control. Moreover, the United Arab Emirates’ National Emergency Crisis and Disaster Management Authority reported that the Dubai flooding resulted from unprecedented rainfall linked to a regional monsoon surge, with no evidence of cloud‑seeding interventions. Authorities continue to monitor misinformation, emphasizing reliance on peer‑reviewed science and official data for accurate weather reporting.
author: Phys.org

title: Rheinmetall Open‑Sources Battlesuite Weapon System Protocol
content:
Rheinmetall has released version 9.10.0 of its Onboard API documentation, now available on the company’s GitHub repository. The update includes new features, bug‑fixes, and expanded examples to aid developers integrating the Onboard API into their applications. The documentation is hosted at https://rheinmetall.github.io/onboardapi-documentation/9.10.0/index, making it freely accessible to the developer community.

The release has generated discussion on Hacker News, where the post (item 49718928) has accumulated 75 points and 13 comments. The conversation highlights interest in the API’s capabilities and the practical guidance provided in the new documentation. Rheinmetall’s continued updates and open‑source approach demonstrate its commitment to supporting external developers and fostering collaboration.

Overall, the 9.10.0 update and the ensuing online discussion illustrate Rheinmetall’s active engagement with the broader tech community, offering developers up‑to‑date resources and a platform for feedback on its Onboard API.
author: Hacker News

title: Haidt's Book Links Social Media to Decline in Teen Mental Health
content:
Jonathan Haidt’s 2022 New York Times bestseller *The Anxious Generation* argues that the surge in smartphone and social‑media use has driven a marked decline in teen mental health since 2010. The book’s thesis quickly became a rallying point for critics of digital platforms, and Haidt has been cited by lawmakers, advocacy groups, and parents as a catalyst for policy action. His arguments have been invoked in public hearings and in court filings against major tech companies, and he has joined forces with bereaved parents who are litigating against social‑media firms.

Haidt’s influence reached international policy circles, most notably in Australia, where his work is credited with shaping the nationwide teen social‑media ban that took effect in 2024. The legislation, which restricts minors’ access to certain platforms, was supported by a coalition of parents, educators, and mental‑health professionals who cited Haidt’s research as evidence of the platforms’ harmful impact. In the United States, several state legislatures have introduced bills limiting data collection from minors and tightening platform accountability, citing Haidt’s findings as part of the evidence base.

While Haidt’s book remains a subject of debate among researchers, its role in galvanizing public and political pressure against social‑media companies is clear. The ongoing legal battles and policy reforms that reference his work underscore a growing trend of scrutinizing digital platforms’ responsibilities toward younger users. As courts and lawmakers continue to evaluate the evidence, Haidt’s narrative will likely remain a touchstone in discussions about technology’s effect on adolescent well‑being.
author: The Verge

title: Microsoft Announces Windows and Surface Event for Oct. 7
content:
Microsoft is set to host a major Windows and Surface event in San Francisco on October 7, marking the first significant PC‑focused gathering in more than two years. The company will use the forum to discuss how local artificial intelligence will shape the next generation of personal computers. Key attendees will include CEO Satya Nadella, Windows and Surface chief Pavan Davuluri, and Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, whose presence hints at a strong emphasis on the RTX Spark PC line.

During the event, Microsoft is expected to reveal new developments for its Surface lineup, including pricing and specifications for the Surface Laptop Ultra. The focus on AI‑powered hardware is likely to be complemented by deeper integration with Nvidia’s GPU technology, positioning the RTX Spark PCs as a central theme. While details remain to be confirmed, the gathering promises to outline a roadmap for Windows and Surface devices that leverages local AI capabilities and advanced graphics performance.
author: The Verge

title: Meta Enables AI Agents to Automate WhatsApp Business Setup
content:
A new WhatsApp Business MCP (Messaging Cloud Platform) server has been launched, enabling developers to integrate advanced AI coding agents such as Claude, Cursor, Codex, and ChatGPT into the WhatsApp Business ecosystem. The update allows these agents to automate key tasks including account setup, creation of messaging templates, end‑to‑end testing, and troubleshooting, streamlining the development workflow for businesses that rely on WhatsApp for customer communication.

The server’s architecture is designed to interface directly with the WhatsApp Business API, providing a secure and scalable environment for AI agents to process and respond to business logic. By leveraging the natural‑language capabilities of the integrated models, developers can reduce manual coding effort, accelerate feature deployment, and improve the reliability of message flows. The update also includes comprehensive documentation and sandbox testing tools to help teams validate their integrations before going live.

Industry analysts view the move as a step toward broader AI adoption in customer‑facing platforms, offering businesses a more efficient way to manage messaging operations. As WhatsApp continues to expand its business services, the integration of AI coding agents is expected to lower the barrier to entry for smaller enterprises and enhance the overall user experience.
author: TechCrunch

title: AI Data Center Expansion Sparks Controversy in Philadelphia's Former Oil Refinery Neighborhood
content:
National outcry over the expansion of data‑center infrastructure has reached Philadelphia, where city officials have acknowledged the possibility of a new facility in a neighborhood already affected by the legacy of a now‑defunct oil refinery. The proposal, which would involve the construction of a large, energy‑intensive data‑center complex, has sparked concern among residents and environmental groups who point to the area’s history of industrial pollution and ongoing remediation efforts. City planners have stated that any development would require a thorough environmental impact assessment and must meet stricter zoning and safety standards than those applied to the former refinery site.

The neighborhood in question, located in the western part of the city, has been the focus of redevelopment initiatives aimed at revitalizing the community after the refinery’s closure in the early 2000s. Local officials have highlighted the need to balance economic growth with public health considerations, noting that data‑center operations can generate significant heat, water usage, and electrical demand. The city’s Department of Planning has indicated that a feasibility study will be conducted to evaluate the site’s suitability, potential infrastructure upgrades, and the projected impact on local traffic and utilities. Community leaders have called for transparent engagement and the inclusion of mitigation plans to address any adverse effects.

While the proposal remains in the preliminary stages, the discussion underscores a growing national debate over the placement of data‑center facilities in historically industrial or environmentally sensitive areas. Philadelphia’s approach, if it moves forward, will likely serve as a case study for how municipalities can navigate the competing demands of technological infrastructure and community well‑being. The city has pledged to keep residents informed as the evaluation process unfolds.
author: TechCrunch

title: Nvidia CEO Says AI Does Not Need New Laws Amid Rising Safety Concerns
content:
Jensen Huang, the chief executive of NVIDIA, reiterated in a keynote at the recent GPU Technology Conference that the company’s hardware and software platforms are engineered with built‑in safety features and that the industry can rely on existing regulatory frameworks to manage the risks of large‑language models and other generative AI systems. Huang stressed that NVIDIA’s AI chips are designed to support secure, auditable workloads and that the firm is working closely with governments to develop standards that will prevent misuse.

In contrast, several current and former employees of the AI‑focused firm OpenAI have publicly warned that safety challenges remain inadequately addressed. Former researcher Ilya Sutskever and current engineer Mira Murati have highlighted concerns about alignment, data privacy, and the potential for rapid deployment of models without sufficient oversight. Their statements, published in industry forums and academic papers, argue that the pace of innovation outstrips the development of robust safety protocols and that additional safeguards are necessary before widespread commercial use.

The divergent views illustrate a broader industry debate over how best to balance rapid AI advancement with responsible deployment. While NVIDIA’s leadership emphasizes collaborative regulation and technical safeguards, OpenAI insiders call for more stringent internal controls and external oversight, underscoring the need for continued dialogue among hardware vendors, software developers, and policymakers.
author: BBC Technology

title: US Redirects $52M Military Aid to Americas
content:
U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio concluded a week‑long tour of South America with a series of meetings in Lima, Bogotá, and Quito, where he met with the conservative administrations of Peru, Colombia, and Ecuador. The trip was aimed at reinforcing U.S. diplomatic ties and outlining a framework for expanded cooperation on security, trade, and regional stability.

During the visits, Rubio and the heads of state discussed a range of issues including counter‑terrorism initiatives, the promotion of free‑trade agreements, and joint efforts to address migration flows. The Secretary pledged additional U.S. support for infrastructure projects, educational exchanges, and technology partnerships, while the South American leaders reaffirmed their commitment to democratic governance and economic reforms. The meetings also touched on the broader strategic context of U.S. engagement in the Western Hemisphere amid shifting geopolitical dynamics.

The outcomes of Rubio’s trip signal a continued U.S. focus on strengthening alliances with key Latin American partners. By securing commitments to deepen cooperation, the U.S. aims to bolster regional security and foster economic growth, while the participating countries seek to enhance their diplomatic and economic ties with Washington.
author: Euronews

title: Céline Dion Returns to Paris Stage After Neurological Disorder
content:
Céline Dion returned to the stage on Saturday, fulfilling a long‑awaited dream after years of battling a rare neurological disorder. The Canadian icon delivered a sell‑out performance at an arena just west of Paris, drawing a full house of fans eager to witness her comeback. The concert marked a significant milestone in her career, as she had been unable to perform publicly since her diagnosis.

During a post‑show interview with FRANCE 24’s Mark Owen, Dion spoke about the emotional weight of the evening and the challenges she has faced. Vocal coach Elena Hurstel echoed this sentiment, noting that the performance was defined by authenticity rather than technical perfection. “We can really see the new Céline,” Hurstel said. “It’s not about being perfect; it’s about being the woman she became, about being real.” The remarks underscored the resilience and renewed artistry that characterized the evening.

The concert’s success signals a hopeful chapter for Dion’s health and career. As she continues her recovery, the event demonstrates her enduring connection to audiences and her determination to return to the spotlight, offering fans a glimpse of her renewed strength and vocal presence.
author: France 24

title: NATO jets down drone over Lithuania, Russian frigate fires flares at Danish helicopter
content:
NATO fighter jets intercepted and destroyed a drone that had entered Lithuanian airspace, while Denmark on Tuesday accused a Russian frigate of firing flares at a Danish military helicopter. The two incidents, which occurred in the Baltic region, have added to the growing tensions along the alliance’s eastern flank.

In Lithuania, the drone was detected by radar and tracked as it crossed the country’s airspace before being shot down by a NATO aircraft. The Lithuanian military confirmed the drone’s presence and the successful interception, noting that no other aircraft were involved. Meanwhile, the Danish helicopter was on a routine training flight when it reported being targeted by flare‑projectiles fired by a Russian warship operating in the area. The Danish Defence Ministry released a statement condemning the act and demanding an explanation from Russia.

These events underscore the heightened security concerns facing NATO members in the eastern part of the alliance. Both incidents illustrate the increasing frequency of provocative actions by Russian naval and aerial assets in proximity to NATO forces, prompting calls for greater vigilance and coordination among member states.
author: France 24

title: Eurozone Citizens Invited to Vote on New Euro Banknote Designs
content:
European citizens have been invited to participate in a public vote on the forthcoming designs of euro banknotes, a move that underscores the EU’s commitment to democratic engagement in monetary policy. The proposed series, slated for circulation around 2030, features a vertical format and highlights historical figures such as Marie Curie and Leonardo da Vinci, alongside contemporary icons. The initiative, announced by the European Central Bank and the European Commission, aims to broaden public input on the aesthetic and symbolic aspects of the euro, with the final designs expected to be approved by the end of 2025.

Amid these developments, rising fuel prices linked to the ongoing Iran conflict have strained consumers across the Eurozone. In southern France, tensions escalated when local fishermen attempted to blockade an oil depot in protest of the price surge. The confrontation, which involved a brief scuffle with police, highlighted the broader economic pressures faced by coastal communities and underscored the immediate impact of geopolitical events on everyday life.

The juxtaposition of these stories illustrates the diverse challenges confronting the Eurozone: a forward‑looking initiative to reshape the currency’s visual identity, coupled with the immediate economic hardships triggered by international conflict. As the public vote proceeds and the fuel crisis continues to affect households, policymakers will need to balance long‑term symbolic reforms with short‑term economic relief measures.
author: France 24

title: China aims to present itself as stabilising force in global politics, expert says
content:
In an interview with France 24’s Monte Francis, Rex Li, a professor of international relations at King’s College London, said China is seeking to promote an alternative international security order and present itself as a stabilising force in global politics. Li noted that Beijing has shown an increasing willingness to assume a more prominent role in resolving the Middle‑East conflict, signalling a shift in its diplomatic posture toward the region.

Despite this expressed intent, Li observed that concrete proposals from China to end the hostilities have yet to materialise.
